_about: Short dated answers to the questions farmers ask search assistants, one block per topic, baked into the page that owns it by scripts/build_ai_answers.py (arc-plc.html by scripts/build_arc_plc.py). Plain text only; every number names its primary source in sources; read = the date we read that copy. The block prints the oldest read date as 'Last checked'. review_by = when the answer goes stale (next report, vote or deadline); the daily site check lists answers past it. A withheld answer renders nothing until its sources are read. Queries from Bing AI Performance, Oct 28, 2026.

answers.question: Where does the 2026 farm bill stand?
text: It has not passed.
The House passed H.R. 7567, the Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026, 224 to 200 on April 30, 2026, and the Senate received it May 19.

The Senate Agriculture Committee reported its own bill, S. 5526, the Agricultural Act of 2026, on September 24, 2026; in the Congress bill record of October 28, its last action is still a place on the Senate calendar, with no floor vote.
Whether the two become one law, and when, is not decided.
ARC, PLC and the higher reference prices do not wait on it: the 2025 law (Pub. L. 119-21) already runs them through the 2031 crop year.

sources.name: FSA ARC/PLC rule, Federal Register, Jan 12, 2026

answers.question: What did the latest USDA crop report say, and when is the next one?
text: The last Crop Production report, out October 9, 2026, put the U.S. corn crop at 16.03 billion bushels on a 181.2 bushel yield, and soybeans at 4.56 billion bushels on 53.1 bushels an acre.

The WASDE out the same day projected 2026/27 ending stocks at 1.849 billion bushels of corn and 315 million bushels of soybeans, with season-average farm prices of $4.70 for corn and $12.00 for soybeans.
The next Crop Production report is Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at noon Eastern (11 a.m. Central), and the last one of 2026 is Thursday, December 10, at the same time.

answers.question: How are tariffs hitting farmers' sales?
text: USDA's October 9 WASDE projects 2026/27 U.S. soybean exports at 1.695 billion bushels, up from 1.515 billion in 2025/26 but still below the 1.892 billion of 2024/25.
Corn exports are projected at 3.300 billion bushels, after 3.429 billion in 2025/26.
USDA puts the 2026/27 season-average farm price at $12.00 for soybeans and $4.70 for corn.
The tariff rates in force and USDA's weekly count of soybeans sold to China are in the sections below; I have not seen a USDA figure for what tariffs cost a farm, so this page does not print one.

answers.question: What is USDA paying farmers for 2025?
text: In 2025 the big one was the Emergency Commodity Assistance Program for the 2024 crop: FSA had paid over $8 billion of its $10 billion by September 26, 2025, when a second payment brought it to 99% of the full rate.

Next is Farmer Bridge Assistance, about $11 billion in one-time payments on 2025 planted acres, at $44.36 an acre for corn, $30.88 for soybeans and $39.35 for wheat (FSA rates of December 31, 2025), paid in 2026.
Both pay on acres, not production; Bridge Assistance has a $155,000 limit per person, and its signup closed April 17, 2026.
Separately, the 2026 ARC and PLC signup runs through December 11, 2026; a farm with no 2026 election by then gets no 2026 payment.

answers.question: Where do cattle markets stand?
text: Today's futures prices are at the top of this page; behind them is a small herd.
NASS counted 94.2 million cattle and calves on U.S. farms on July 1, 2026, with 28.5 million beef cows, down 1% from a year earlier, and a 2026 calf crop of 32.5 million head, down 2%.
USDA's October 9 WASDE left its cattle price forecasts unchanged and puts the 2026 average 5-area fed steer price at $237.56 per cwt, against $224.37 in 2025; that is a forecast.

answers.question: Is there a beef shortage?
text: There is less U.S. beef, and imports are filling part of the gap.

USDA's October 9 WASDE forecasts 2026 U.S. beef production at 24.87 billion pounds, down 4.6% from 26.07 billion in 2025, and cut it from September on fewer steers and heifers going to slaughter and lighter carcasses.
Beef imports are forecast at 6.35 billion pounds, up 17.8% from 5.39 billion, and beef use per person at 58.9 pounds, against 59.2 in 2025.

sources.name: USDA WASDE-676, Oct 9, 2026 (U.S. meats supply and use)

answers.question: How much Argentine beef can come into the U.S.?
text: Argentina has its own U.S. beef quota of 20,000 tons a year, at a $44 a ton duty inside it and 26.4% above it, and the U.S. took 42,445 tons of Argentine beef in 2025, the most since 1999 (FAS, March 9, 2026).
For 2026 only, Proclamation 11010 added 80,000 metric tons for Argentina, limited to lean beef trimmings and opened in four 20,000-ton quarters; the last one runs October 1 to December 31, 2026.

The 300,000 tons of extra lean trimmings added in August by Proclamation 11059 went to other countries, not Argentina, and its last tranche closes when filled or on November 30, 2026, whichever comes first.
Whether any of it is extended into 2027 is not decided.

sources.name: FAS GAIN, Argentina Livestock and Products, Mar 9, 2026

answers.question: What does New World screwworm mean for cattle prices?
text: The price effect runs through the border: cattle from Mexico were shut out over New World screwworm from November 22, 2024, and USDA then raised its 2025 forecast for 750 to 800 pound feeder steers by $15 to $272.50 per cwt, a forecast, not a measured effect (ERS, December 16, 2024).
USDA is now reopening border ports to Mexican cattle in phases: Santa Teresa, NM on September 24, 2026, Columbus, NM on October 26, and Nogales, AZ planned for November 30.
Inside the U.S., APHIS confirmed the first wildlife case on October 21, 2026, an elk on a game ranch in Pecos County, Texas, and Texas is changing its infested zone around it.
APHIS keeps the case count and the zone map on its status page, linked below.

sources.name: ERS Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry Outlook, Dec 16, 2024
APHIS, current status of New World screwworm

answers.question: Is there a USDA heifer retention program?
text: Not as a cash program.

What USDA announced on August 31, 2026 is BRAND (Beef Retention and National Development), a proposed endorsement to Livestock Risk Protection insurance that would insure the value of keeping a heifer for breeding over two years.

It would set a protected value from the heifer's expected slaughter value at enrollment and pay the difference if her projected or realized slaughter value rises above what she is worth kept as breeding stock.
It is not on offer yet: on October 13, 2026 the crop insurance board approved an outside expert review of the LRP breeding cattle submission, not the policy itself.
No premium, payment rate, eligibility rule or signup date is in the USDA and board documents I read.
